To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the sintered hydroxyl- and phosphate-poor hydroxyapatite (HA) forms bonelike apatie by undergoing the same structural changes, i.e., formation of a Ca-rich and Ca-poor amorphous or nanocrystalline calcium phosphates (Ca-ACP) and a crystallization into bonelike Apatite, but at a lower rate than does the HA sintering at 800 degreesC, due to its initial lower surface negativity.

the HA surface undergoes a surface structural change, which is the formation of a Ca-rich and a Ca-pour ACP, which crystallizes into bonelike ACP, during the process of apatite formation, and that the sintered temperature might influence the rate of the process.

the sintering of hydroxyapatite (HA) at 800 degreesC and 1200degreesC, respectively, in air for 3h results in a surface structure change, i.e. formation of a Ca-rich and a Ca-pore amorphous calcium phosphate (ACP), which eventually crystallized to a bonelike apaitite with a low dissolution rate in simulated body fluid.

the process and kinetics of boned-like apatite formation, which is the first step of bone bonding, on the HA surface in the SBF.

the process of bonelike surface apatite formation and its kinetics, which is important to the understanding of the mechanism of bone growth onto biomaterials.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
sintering temperature does not influence the formation of bonelike ACP on HA but the rate of formation, which in turn affects the rate of apatite formation and the surface charge of HA.

the process and kinetics of bonlike apatite formation are the same for all the sintered HA, whereas the rate of bonelike formation is different, depending on the surface charge and hence the sintering temperature of the HA.

the HA sintering process at 800 degrees or 1200 degrees degrees C does not alter the process but only the rate of formation, of bonelike hydroxyapatite on the HA surface, through which HA can integrate with living bone.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sintered temperature might be a key factor to control the rate of formation and thus the time for the HA to be integrated with the bone.

bonelike apatiite is formed on sintered HA by the process of forming Ca-rich amorphouos calcium phosphate (ACP), followed by the formation of Ca-poor ACD and then the crystallization of Ca-poor APC into bonelike ACP, and the process is influenced by surface charge of sintered HA.
the sintered HA with a lower negative surface charge is expected to form bonelike ACP on its surface at a faster rate, thereby being a better bone substitute.
The main takeaway from our work is that

sintering of HA at a temperature higher than 1000 degrees C is recommended for the fabrication of HA-based biomaterials to enhance the rate of bonelike-apatite formation on their surfaces, thereby promoting the integration of the materials with living bone.
HA sintered below 1200 degreesC is more suitable for bone tissue engineering applications than the HA sinterd at higher temperatures.
sintered hydroxyl apatites can be a potential candidate of biomaterials for bone repair.
